claim: On the space station a burning fuel droplet seemed to go out but kept burning with no visible flame, so the fire went out twice: once with a visible flame and once without.
quote: A fuel droplet appeared to extinguish but actually continued to burn without a visible flame. The fire went out twice—once with and once without a visible flame.
source_title: 20 Breakthroughs from 20 Years of Science aboard the International Space Station: Discovery of steadily burning cool flames
source_org: NASA (International Space Station Program Science Office)
locator: section 'Discovery of steadily burning cool flames', paragraph 2
limits: A NASA summary page, not the primary paper: it gives no oxygen level, pressure or droplet size. It describes a liquid fuel droplet in a closed chamber, not a solid material or a real cargo fire.
verifier_note: evtool found:true. In context the next sentence says 'large droplets of heptane fuel' and the second stage was 'sustained by what is known as cool flame chemical heat release', which matches the conditions. Page dated 26 Oct 2020. Claim does not generalise beyond a droplet in a closed chamber.

claim: Cool flames that burn without fuel and air being premixed were discovered in 2012 aboard the space station during the FLEX droplet studies.
quote: Non-premixed cool flames, created when fuel and oxidizer are not mixed before reacting, were discovered in 2012 aboard the space station during the Flame Extinguishment (FLEX) studies, helping spawn a rapidly growing research field into the nature of cool flames.
source_title: Cool Flames Created During a First for International Space Station Research

conditions.fuel: liquid fuel droplets in 2012 (gaseous fuels in the 2021 CFI-G follow-up)

limits: Gives the year only; none of the NASA pages I opened gives the date of the first observation. NASA's 2012 release (an Old Theory Goes up in Cool Flames, 27 Aug 2012) says the findings were already 'in press' in Combustion and Flame by then. The follow-up in the same article burned gaseous fuels on a burner, not droplets.
verifier_note: evtool found:true. Page dated 16 Jul 2021 (Erin Winick Anthony). 'Liquid droplets' in the claim is supported by the same article: 'the flames created aboard station in 2012 burned liquid fuel'. Year only, as the limits say.

claim: Cool flames have been made on Earth but flicker out quickly, while on the space station they can burn for minutes.
quote: Cool flames have been produced on Earth, but they quickly flicker out. On station, cool flames can burn for minutes, giving scientists a better opportunity to study them.
source_title: 20 Breakthroughs from 20 Years of Science aboard the International Space Station: Discovery of steadily burning cool flames
source_org: NASA (International Space Station Program Science Office)
locator: section 'Discovery of steadily burning cool flames', 'Why do this in space?'

conditions.gravity: microgravity on the ISS versus Earth gravity

limits: NASA gives no number for 'quickly' and does not say which Earth experiments it means (Nayagam et al. 2014, NTRS 20140006750, p. 2, says earlier Earth cool-flame work used stirred reactors, flow reactors, shock tubes and rapid compression machines, all 'primarily' premixed gases). A separate NASA article (16 July 2021, nasa.gov) goes further: cool flames 'are nearly impossible to create in Earth's gravity'. Neither page tests a fire in cargo.
verifier_note: evtool found:true. Quote is under 'Why do this in space?' on the 20 Breakthroughs page (26 Oct 2020). The comparison is NASA's own wording; no number for 'quickly'. Limit about earlier Earth work being premixed gases confirmed in Nayagam 2014 p. 2 ('All these studies primarily involved premixed gases').

claim: In a computer simulation of a weightless flame fed by gaseous heptane, no cool flame appeared alongside the hot flame, because oxygen could not reach the burner surface: the hot flame used it up, or airflow worked against the oxygen's diffusion.
quote: because the oxygen cannot penetrate to the burner surface due to the consumption by the high-temperature flame or the convection against the oxygen diffusion.
source_title: Combustion Characteristics in a Non-Premixed Cool-Flame Regime of n-Heptane in Microgravity
source_authors: Fumiaki Takahashi, Viswanath R. Katta, Michael C. Hicks
source_org: Case Western Reserve University; Innovative Scientific Solutions Inc.; NASA Glenn Research Center (9th U.S. National Combustion Meeting, 17-20 May 2015)

conditions.pressure_text: not stated in the text I read
conditions.flow_text: still air to 10 mm/s air stream (simulated: 3 mm/s gives flame pulsation, 4-10 mm/s a steady locally extinguished flame)
conditions.fuel: gaseous n-heptane from a porous burner (simulated, 127 species, 1130 reactions)

limits: A simulation of a gas-fuelled porous burner in zero gravity (127 species, 1130 reactions), not a droplet experiment, not a measurement and not an Earth flame. The paper does not simulate Earth buoyant flows, so 'on Earth buoyancy removes the cool flame' is the story's inference, not this paper's finding. The first half of the sentence ('The computation does not show the low-temperature cool flame co-existing with the high-temperature diffusion flame (either the stable, locally extinguished, or pulsating flames)') reads verbatim in the PDF but cannot be machine-matched across a line-break hyphen, so the checked quote starts mid-sentence.
verifier_note: evtool found:true on the (mid-sentence) quote. Source gives TWO reasons, joined by 'or': the hot flame consuming the oxygen, or convection against oxygen diffusion; and it lists 'stable, locally extinguished, or pulsating flames', so 'when air flowed past' was too narrow. Claim reworded to follow the source. Locator corrected: item 8 is on PDF p. 10 (Conclusions begin p. 9), not 'starts on p. 9'.

claim: In the same simulation, once the hot flame died the surroundings cooled, oxygen moved in to the fuel source and the low-temperature cool-flame regime began.
quote: After the radiative extinction of the high-temperature diffusion flame occurs at t = 7 s, the temperature decreases in the entire field, thus the oxygen penetrates into the near-burner region, and the low-temperature cool-flame regime begins.
source_title: Combustion Characteristics in a Non-Premixed Cool-Flame Regime of n-Heptane in Microgravity
source_authors: Fumiaki Takahashi, Viswanath R. Katta, Michael C. Hicks
source_org: Case Western Reserve University; Innovative Scientific Solutions Inc.; NASA Glenn Research Center (9th U.S. National Combustion Meeting, 17-20 May 2015)

conditions.pressure_text: not stated in the text I read
conditions.flow_text: near-quiescent air (abstract gives a speed limit of about 2 mm/s)
conditions.fuel: gaseous n-heptane from a porous burner (simulated)

limits: A simulation with a gaseous fuel source, not a droplet and not a measurement; the 7 s timing belongs to that run. It explains why a second, cooler burn can start but does not show it for cargo materials.
verifier_note: evtool found:true. Context (Section 3, 'Two-Stage Combustion', PDF p. 4) is the quiescent-air run: radiative extinction at t = 7 s, then the 700 K cool-flame regime next to the fuel source. The claim says 'in the same simulation' and the limits state it is gaseous fuel, simulated, not a droplet. Abstract hedges the regime as 'typically followed by' a transition; the claim does not overstate it.

limits: 'Invisible' refers to the cameras used in these first FLEX tests. The same abstract says the new burning regime was verified by theoretical and numerical analysis, and radiometers also registered heat (Nayagam et al. 2014, NTRS 20140006750, p. 4). Later NASA material (Nayagam et al., NTRS 20160000344) says the cool flame was imaged once the hardware was changed (spectral filters removed, backlight turned down, 10-20 frame averages: 'QS cool flame visualized for the first time'). Liquid heptane (and methanol) droplets only; free author-hosted copy of the published article.
story_use: why it is hard to notice
verifier_note: evtool found:true. Two overstatements removed: (1) the source says 'the experiment imaging system', not 'the station's cameras'; (2) 'only because the droplet kept burning' is too strong: the same abstract says verification came from theoretical and numerical analysis, and Nayagam et al. 2014 (radiometers) also measured the heat. Gravity '<1e-5 g' confirmed on p. 4 (SAMS data, 'typically less than 10^-5 g0'). Landing URL is an author-hosted copy at Cornell; the paper's DOI (10.1007/s12217-014-9372-2) resolves.

claim: In one n-decane droplet test, the droplet's burning-rate constant (how fast its diameter squared shrinks) was 0.41 mm2/s with the visible flame and 0.33 mm2/s in the cool-flame stage the cameras could not see, about four-fifths as fast.
quote: The burning rate constants K (=dD2 /dt) corresponding to the first and second stage combustion were found to be 0.41 and 0.33 mm2 /s respectively.
source_title: Cool-flame extinction during n-alkane droplet combustion in microgravity
source_authors: V. Nayagam, D. Dietrich, M. C. Hicks, F. A. Williams
source_org: NASA Glenn Research Center; Case Western Reserve University; UC San Diego (Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Spring Technical Meeting, 16-18 March 2014)
locator: Section 3.1 (N-decane results), p. 4, Fig. 1a, test R377

conditions.fuel: n-decane droplet, 4.03 mm initial diameter (test R377), in 79% nitrogen

limits: One test of one fuel. K is how fast the droplet's diameter squared shrinks, not a direct measure of heat. The 'four-fifths' (0.33/0.41) is my arithmetic. Other tests in the same paper: 0.31 and 0.27 mm2/s at 17% oxygen; 0.29 and 0.25 mm2/s at 14% oxygen. Liquid droplet only.
verifier_note: evtool found:true. Numbers confirmed in Section 3.1 for test R377 (n-decane, D0 = 4.03 mm, 21% O2 / 79% N2, 0.5 atm, PDF p. 4): K = 0.41 then 0.33 mm2/s. Claim reworded to say what K is (rate of fall of the droplet diameter squared) instead of implying a shrinking speed in mm2/s; 'four-fifths' is 0.33/0.41 = 0.80 (arithmetic, flagged). The quote itself does not name the fuel or the test; that comes from the paragraph just before it. A journal version exists (Combust. Flame, DOI 10.1016/j.combustflame.2015.01.012, listed in PSI-39/68/69); its numbers were not checked.

claim: During the cool-flame stage the colour and ultraviolet cameras were not sensitive enough to register any flame image, but radiometers still measured heat radiating from the droplet, which the authors read as active chemical heat release.
quote: Both the color camera and the UV-camera are not sensitive enough to register any flame images during this period. Both the broadband and narrowband radiometers, however, register continued radiative heat loss from the droplet indicating active chemical heat release.
source_title: Cool-flame extinction during n-alkane droplet combustion in microgravity
source_authors: V. Nayagam, D. Dietrich, M. C. Hicks, F. A. Williams
source_org: NASA Glenn Research Center; Case Western Reserve University; UC San Diego (Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Spring Technical Meeting, 16-18 March 2014)

conditions.fuel: n-decane droplet, 4.03 mm initial diameter (test R377)

limits: Radiometers show that heat is being radiated; they do not give a temperature or say which chemicals are made. 'Active chemical heat release' is the authors' interpretation. Even a sensitive intensified camera with a formaldehyde filter produced poor images of the cool flame in later tests (Farouk et al., NTRS 20190002838, p. 3). Liquid droplet in a closed chamber.
story_use: why it is hard to notice
verifier_note: evtool found:true. Same test R377. The source says the cameras 'are not sensitive enough to register any flame images' and that the radiometers' continued heat loss is 'indicating active chemical heat release'. The claim's 'showing it was still burning' was firmer than the source's 'indicating'; reworded to attribute the reading to the authors.

claim: NASA describes a cool flame as burning at about 600 degrees Celsius, against about 1,400 degrees Celsius for a typical candle.
quote: A cool flame is one that burns at about 600 degrees Celsius. To understand how cool this is, consider that a typical candle is about two-and-a-half times hotter, burning at around 1,400 degrees Celsius.
source_title: International Space Station Benefits for Humanity, 2nd Edition: Cool flame research aboard space station may lead to a cleaner environment on Earth
locator: printed p. 81 (PDF p. 95), section 'Cool flame research aboard space station may lead to a cleaner environment on Earth'
limits: A rounded, popular figure, not a measured droplet temperature. NASA's own wording of the ratio varies: 'two-and-a-half times' here (and in a 2020 NASA page) but 600 vs 1,400 C is about 2.3x, and a NASA ISS daily report of 20 Aug 2021 says 'about two times hotter'. Simulations give a cool-stage peak gas temperature of about 700 K (about 430 C) (Dietrich et al. 2014) and about 765 K at elevated pressure with helium (Farouk et al. 2018); no source I opened measured a droplet cool flame directly.
verifier_note: evtool found:true. Locator corrected: the sentence is on printed p. 81 (PDF p. 95), not pp. 81-82. Claim text is a faithful report of NASA's wording and is attributed ('NASA describes'). Caution for the story: this is a popular round figure that conflicts with NASA-funded simulations (about 700 K = 430 C in Dietrich et al. 2014 and Takahashi et al. 2015; 765 K in Farouk et al. 2018), and '2.5 times' does not match 1,400/600 = 2.3. NASA's ISS daily report of 20 Aug 2021 (nasa.gov/blogs/stationreport) says 'about two times hotter' (confirmed in a search excerpt). Use only as NASA's description, never as a measured droplet temperature.

claim: NASA says ordinary flames make soot, carbon dioxide and water, while cool flames make carbon monoxide and formaldehyde.
quote: Typical flames produce soot, carbon dioxide, and water. Cool flames produce carbon monoxide and formaldehyde.
source_title: 20 Breakthroughs from 20 Years of Science aboard the International Space Station: Discovery of steadily burning cool flames
source_org: NASA (International Space Station Program Science Office)
locator: section 'Discovery of steadily burning cool flames', 'Why does it matter?'
limits: A one-line NASA summary, with no amounts, no toxicity levels and no in-orbit gas measurement on the page. The page frames it as a reason to study cleaner engines, not as a crew hazard. A simulation (Farouk et al. 2018) lists formaldehyde, acetaldehyde and other partly burned compounds 'present at high concentrations during the third-stage cool flame burn' and CO turning into CO2 'substantially inhibited' at the warmer (about 970 K) stage; that is modelled n-heptane, not measured.
story_use: what it does to people and equipment
verifier_note: evtool found:true (15 words). Quote verbatim from 'Why does it matter?'. NASA frames it as chemically different flames for cleaner engines, not as a crew hazard; limits already say so. Farouk 2018 statements quoted in limits confirmed in its text (formaldehyde and acetaldehyde 'present at high concentrations during the third-stage Cool flame burn'; CO to CO2 'substantially inhibited' in the Warm flame).

claim: Around the time the cool flame ended (just before or just after), a vapour cloud formed around the droplet; the authors describe it as partially oxidized fuel and other products that condensed.
quote: A vapor cloud was also found to form around the droplet as the partially oxidized fuel and other products condensed just prior to or immediately following cool flame extinction.
source_title: Cool-flame extinction during n-alkane droplet combustion in microgravity
source_authors: V. Nayagam, D. Dietrich, M. C. Hicks, F. A. Williams
source_org: NASA Glenn Research Center; Case Western Reserve University; UC San Diego (Central States Section of the Combustion Institute, Spring Technical Meeting, 16-18 March 2014)
locator: Section 1, Introduction, PDF p. 2 (summary of earlier FLEX observations); abstract p. 1 says the cloud formed 'in most cases'
limits: The cloud was seen by cameras; what it is made of is inferred. The introduction sentence summarises earlier FLEX results; in this paper's own tests the abstract says it formed 'in most cases', not always. Dietrich et al. 2014 say a model predicts 'gaseous pure fuel vapor in addition to larger alkenes, ketohydroperoxides and cyclic ethers' that 'could condense'; a NASA-funded simulation (Takahashi et al. 2015) points to a fuel and water mixture. Neither says whether the cloud is toxic or flammable. Liquid droplets only.
story_use: what it does to people and equipment
verifier_note: evtool found:true. Source says the cloud formed 'just prior to or immediately following' cool-flame extinction, so 'when the cool flame ended' was too exact; reworded. The sentence is in the Introduction and summarises the earlier FLEX observations (ref. [3]); this paper's own abstract adds that the cloud formed 'in most cases', i.e. not always. Composition is inferred, as the limits say.

claim: A 2012 NASA Glenn release says that, because the flame keeps burning after the hot flame goes out, fire suppression techniques will need to consider that the pure-fuel flame may not really be out even with no visible flame, and that it could behave like a smouldering solid that re-ignites into open flame.
quote: Since the flame continues to produce combustion after the hot-flame goes out, fire suppression techniques will need to consider the possibility that the pure-fuel flame is not really out, even with no visible flame. It could behave like a solid that smolders and reignites into open flame under the right conditions, leading to the need for space-specific suppression techniques.
source_title: An Old Theory Goes up in Cool Flames
source_authors: NASA Glenn Research Center (press contacts Katherine Martin, Mike Giannone)
source_org: NASA Glenn Research Center (release JR12-009), republished by 24-7 Press Release Newswire
locator: paragraph beginning 'Fire safety in space can also benefit from this new discovery'
limits: SECONDARY HOST: a wire-service copy of NASA's release; the original nasa.gov page (nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/news/cool_flame.html, 27 Aug 2012) now returns 404 and the Wayback capture could not be opened here. NASA's forward-looking statement, not a test result. 'Behave like a solid that smolders' is an analogy: no solid material was burned in FLEX.
story_use: what it does to people and equipment
verifier_note: evtool found:true on the 24-7 PressRelease copy only. I could not open the Wayback capture (web.archive.org is blocked from this environment; 403/connection reset) and nasa.gov/mission_pages/station/research/news/cool_flame.html returns 404, so landing_url now points at the page I verified. It is a wire-service republication of NASA Glenn release JR12-009 (13 Sept 2012; NASA Glenn contacts Katherine Martin / Mike Giannone), and NASA's own '20 Breakthroughs' page links to the nasa.gov original under the same title, so the text is very likely identical. Marked as secondary host. Claim wording aligned with the source ('will need to consider the possibility').

claim: In space-station n-dodecane droplet tests at elevated pressure with helium added, the authors report that hot-flame burning can restart from the cooler 'warm flame' stage.
quote: Similar experiments using n-dodecane as fuel indicate that re-initiation of hot flame burning from the “Warm flame” condition can occur when the heat release/loss balance results in reaction temperatures exceeding the NTC “hot ignition” condition.
source_title: Three stage cool flame droplet burning behavior of n-alkane droplets at elevated pressure conditions: Hot, warm and cool flame
source_authors: T. I. Farouk, D. Dietrich, F. L. Dryer
source_org: University of South Carolina; NASA Glenn Research Center; Princeton University (International Symposium on Combustion, Dublin, 29 July-3 August 2018)
locator: Section 5, Summary (PDF p. 8); run in Fig. 7 and Section 4 text (PDF p. 8-9)
investigation: FLEX/CFI droplet series, Combustion Integrated Rack (run label 'FLEX 1268'); the paper does not name the PSI record (PSI-39 CFI lists n-dodecane work)
limits: Warm-to-hot, not cool-to-hot, seen at elevated pressure (2.75 atm) with helium in the run shown; the paper's own n-dodecane simulation did not predict it. 'Can occur' is the authors' reading of limited runs. The authors also write that heat feedback through the tether fibre 'can play a substantial role in this behavior' and that 'other external sources of perturbation can also trigger this phenomenon', so the restart may be partly a test-hardware effect. Liquid droplet only; it does not show a cool flame re-igniting a solid or a cargo fire. A NASA-funded simulation of a gaseous-fuel cool flame (Takahashi et al. 2015) also predicts a 'flash reignition' after about 18 s.
story_use: what it does to people and equipment
verifier_note: evtool found:true. Quote is on PDF p. 8 (Section 5, Summary). The Section 4 text for run FLEX 1268 (Fig. 7, 2.75 atm, 21% O2, 29% He, n-dodecane 4.35 mm) states 'a re-initiation and radiant extinction of hot flame burning is also observed', so it is an observation. The authors' wording is 'can occur', so 'sometimes restarted' is softened to match. The paper does not name the investigation (run label 'FLEX 1268'), so the PSI id was an assumption; PSI-39 (CFI) lists n-dodecane work but I could not confirm the link from this paper. IMPORTANT caveat added to limits: the same section says heat feedback through the tether fibre 'can play a substantial role in this behavior' and 'other external sources of perturbation can also trigger this phenomenon', so the restart may be partly a test-hardware effect.

source_org: NASA Glenn Research Center (14th U.S. National Combustion Meeting, 16-19 March 2025, poster abstract)

conditions.fuel: liquid droplets; gaseous fuels; solid fuels (PMMA)

limits: Covers experiments in the Combustion Integrated Rack only, as described in a poster abstract (14th US National Combustion Meeting, March 2025). It shows which fuel types each programme used, not what was found. The same abstract says non-premixed cool flames were discovered in droplet research and later seen with gaseous fuel on a burner; none of the sources checked reports a cool flame from a solid material or cargo item, so the story must not claim it.

The abstract is about experiments in the Combustion Integrated Rack (14 independent experiments as of March 2025), not all ISS combustion work, and 'only now' is not in the source (it says 'the current series'); claim narrowed to the CIR and to the source's wording. source_authors: V. Nayagam, D. Dietrich, M. C. Hicks, F. A. Williams

limits: Droplets about 1.5 to 5 mm across in a roughly 95-litre closed chamber with a hot-wire igniter. NASA's 2012 release says the two-stage burn 'was not seen in smaller heptane droplets that were less than 2.4 mm in size'. Nothing here says what size, shape or material of a real fuel load would do the same.

verifier_note: evtool found:true (abstract, PDF p. 1). 'Disruptively extinguished' was rendered as 'broke apart'; the source's own words are kept. 'Large' is relative: droplets were about 1.5 to 5 mm in this paper. Claim also restricted to n-alkane droplets, which is what the abstract says.
